The Estuary cobbler (Cnidoglanis macrocephalus) reaches a maximum total length of 91 cm [Li = 91 cm], making it one of the larger representatives within the family Plotosidae. However, the onset of reproductive maturity occurs at a considerably smaller size, with individuals attaining a total length of 41 cm [Lp = 41 cm] at puberty. This disparity between size at maturation and ultimate body length is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction, a pattern observed in several other estuarine-dwelling teleosts facing variable environmental conditions. Hatched from adhesive, demersal eggs that measure approximately 7 mm in diameter, the prolarvae emerge after an incubation period that is strongly temperature-dependent. At a stable water temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], eclosion occurs after approximately 44.5 days [ab = approximately 44.5 days], a duration that reflects the relatively slow developmental rate imposed by the cool, thermally stable conditions typical of the species' deeper estuarine habitats.

Upon hatching, the yolk-sac larva, or alevin, carries a modest endowment of endogenous reserves, with the wet weight at birth recorded at 0.18 grams [Wwb = 0.18 grams]. This remarkably low neonatal mass is a direct consequence of the small egg size and highlights the vulnerability of the prolarvae during the lecithotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding. The rapid depletion of yolk nutrients necessitates a timely trophic switch, as the mouth-closed larva must transition to first exogenous feeding before the point of no return is reached. Following successful yolk-sac resorption and the commencement of active foraging, the free-swimming larva enters a planktonic phase characterized by rapid mass gain. In the controlled conditions typical of a hatchery setting maintained at 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], the period between egg fertilisation and the emergence of the yolk-sac larva is consistent with the approximately 44.5 days [ab = approximately 44.5 days] required for incubation, underscoring the synchrony between embryonic development and the subsequent larval growth window.

Individuals that survive the vulnerable larval and early juvenile stages undergo a pronounced allometric shift during the larval-juvenile transition, ultimately approaching a maximum adult body mass that is considerable for the species. The ultimate wet weight attained by adults is 4720 grams [Wwi = 4720 grams], a size that reflects the substantial somatic investment required to achieve the maximum recorded total length of 91 cm [Li = 91 cm]. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty is reported as 408.5 grams [Wwp = 408.5 grams], indicating that females initiate vitellogenesis and males commence spermatogenesis at a body mass less than ten percent of the ultimate possible mass. This early pubertal mass, relative to the ultimate wet weight, suggests that the Estuary cobbler adopts a risk-spreading reproductive tactic, enabling individuals to contribute to the next generation even if they do not survive to achieve maximal size. Field surveys and captive growth studies have corroborated this ontogenetic pattern consistently.

The species' life-history schedule appears finely tuned to the thermal regime of its environment. The maximum lifespan documented for Cnidoglanis macrocephalus in the wild is 13 years [am = 13 years] under a sustained thermal regime of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], a longevity that is relatively extended for a fish of its ultimate size and that allows for multiple spawning events across several seasons. In females that attain a length of 200 cm, a size that is exceptionally rare and well beyond the typical adult maximum, the reproductive output is substantial. At a stable water temperature of 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C], such a large female produces approximately 7483 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 7483 eggs per spawning event], occurring at a rate of approximately 1 spawning event per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 spawning event per year], a fecundity that reflects the exponential increase in reproductive output with body size and that underscores the considerable contribution of the oldest and largest individuals to population recruitment.

Comparative analyses with other plotosid catfishes reveal that the Estuary cobbler's pubertal length of 41 cm [Lp = 41 cm] is intermediate among its congeners, falling between the earlier-maturing freshwater species and the later-maturing marine forms. This pattern likely reflects the variable predation pressures and resource availability characteristic of estuarine environments. The maximum adult body mass of 4720 grams [Wwi = 4720 grams] is similarly intermediate, positioning the species as a moderately sized member of the family. The 13-year lifespan (13 years) [am = 13 years] at 18.2 °C [T = 18.2 °C] is noteworthy because it allows for repeated, iteroparous spawning cycles across a decade or more, a life-history strategy that buffers against poor recruitment years common in fluctuating estuarine systems. Field evidence suggests that post-reproductive senescence may contribute to natural mortality in the oldest individuals, completing a life cycle that begins with a single 0.18 gram [Wwb = 0.18 gram] larva and ends after more than a decade of growth and reproduction.
